description:
🚀 We are Orbit Flame, an aerospace team from Tashkent building Fluxion-A1, a solid fuel rocket.

🔥 Why "Flame in Freefall"? Fire is our expertise. We study how fuel burns every day.

🎯 Our goal: turn microgravity fire data into safety insights for astronauts.

🛠 We bring: propellant chemistry, nozzle physics, aerodynamics.

💻 We need: Coding, AI/ML, Data Analysis.

Join us and solve a real space problem!
summary:
Fire is one of the scariest things that can happen on a spacecraft, and flames behave very differently without gravity. NASA has run many experiments on this, but the data is scattered across long reports and files that are hard to read and compare.

So we built Flame in Freefall, a dashboard with an AI assistant on top of it. We went through NASA's PSI research documents and pulled 23 combustion and fire-safety experiments into one organized database. For each one you can see the fuel, oxygen level, pressure, airflow, gravity level, sensors, hardware and key results. If something wasn't in the documents, we marked it "unknown" and did not guess. Every entry is also marked unverified until a teammate checks it.

With the dashboard, you can filter and compare experiments in a few clicks. The AI helps you find what you need without reading dozens of papers. We also checked each experiment against expected Moon-base conditions, like higher oxygen and pressure up to 10.2 psi, to show which results might carry over to future lunar missions.

We think this matters because safer spaceships and Moon bases need fire designs built on real microgravity data.
details:
Flame in Freefall Explorer is an interactive web platform created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The project investigates how fire behaves in microgravity and partial-gravity environments, including the International Space Station, the Moon, Mars, and spacesuit operations.

The main purpose of the platform is to make complex space-combustion research easier to understand through interactive visualizations, simulations, and NASA-based investigation data. Users can explore real combustion experiments, search and filter research topics, compare different investigations, and examine their relevance to future space missions.

The platform includes a mission simulator that analyzes atmospheric conditions such as oxygen concentration, cabin pressure, and gravity. Based on these parameters, it provides an estimated fire hazard level and recommends relevant NASA investigations. The interactive flame laboratory also demonstrates how flame shape, spread rate, temperature, and extinction behavior change depending on gravity, airflow, oxygen levels, and fuel materials.

Another important feature is the research assistant, which explains topics such as cool flames, smoke-particle behavior, spacecraft fire risks, and flame suppression methods. The project uses curated NASA research content to provide educational explanations and mission-focused insights.

Flame in Freefall Explorer was built using React, Vite, Three.js, JavaScript, CSS, GSAP, Motion, and Lucide React. It is designed for students, researchers, engineers, astronauts, and anyone interested in space science and fire safety.

The simulator provides educational estimates and should not replace official NASA procedures or professional engineering analysis.
